papers.title: The accessible human surfaceome
papers.abstract: Proteins associated with the extracellular face of the plasma membrane ("surface proteins" or the "surfaceome") are important therapeutic targets because they can direct therapeutics to specific cell types and deliver them into cells. However, experimental and computational databases disagree substantially on which proteins make up the human plasma membrane proteome, and none focus specifically on the set of accessible surface proteins that would be useful for therapeutic applications. Here, we used an agentic LLM pipeline to curate the accessible human surfaceome from literature. To assess performance, we built SurfaceBench, a manually curated benchmark of 147 proteins on which five reference databases frequently disagree. Our LLM triage agent classified surface status more accurately than existing databases and recovered 1,108 candidate surface proteins not present in any of them. On held-out clinical and viral-entry surface targets, the pipeline recovered 98-100% of established surface antigens. A literature-anchored deep-dive pipeline run on over 5,000 candidates then returned 1,783 canonical surface proteins and 1,252 with weaker or context-dependent surface evidence. Each queryable record contains 24 LLM-based annotation fields--including confidence, primary localization, and expression breadth--and seven deterministic structural and topological features. Unlike existing databases, our records trace every claim to the agent's reasoning and to exact quotes from the full-text literature it could access. All records can be browsed in an open-source viewer. These results show that LLMs reasoning over unstructured scientific text can build updatable, bespoke databases that outperform expert-curated resources, although performance remains limited by agent access to full-text literature.

papers.title: Auditing Confidence-Calibrated Benchmarking of Single-Cell Perturbation Models
papers.abstract: Single-cell perturbation models are increasingly assessed for both predictive performance and calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. We constructed such an evaluation harness (two datasets, Norman 2019 and Replogle 2022; four split types over six dataset-split combinations; three models, scVI, CPA and a linear Ridge baseline; three uncertainty quantification methods, MC dropout, quantile regression and split conformal prediction) and then audited it against null baselines it had never included. Most of its headline results measure something other than what their metric names claim. The harness supplied each test cell to the model as input and then scored the model on reproducing that same cell's expression, so an identity predictor returning the input unchanged attains a perturbation-effect correlation of 1.0 on all six splits: any model given the target cell is measured against this echo ceiling rather than against a null. Against a constant train-mean predictor, scVI wins on 99.7% of Norman cells but only 0.2% of Replogle cells. One split held out sequencing batches rather than perturbations; another scores no genuinely novel perturbation after label collapse; unseen perturbations are silently replaced with a negative-control sentinel at inference; and the most convention-sensitive decision-value entry moves 29.2 percentage points under a library-size convention that changes that row's all-gene MSE by 0.01%. Because a validation budget is spent on a ranked shortlist rather than on a marginal interval, we also score each uncertainty signal by the DE-gene error it avoids in the top k: the worst-calibrated method is the best ranker, and a benchmark reporting only coverage orders the two backwards. We document six failure modes, each with its mechanism, the diagnostic that exposes it, and a detection procedure transferable to other harnesses. One result survives, with a boundary condition: split-conformal coverage calibrated on K562 residuals under-covers on RPE1 (0.900 to 0.847), and marginal coverage at the nominal 0.900 is compatible with covering 0.271 to 0.342 of the DE-gene intervals a prioritization decision would rest on. We continue to recommend conformal prediction, recalibrated per cellular context and reported per gene set rather than marginally.

papers.title: N-Zinclopedia: A database of predicted transition metal-binding sites and metalloenzymes
papers.abstract: Metal ions are among the most common enzymatic cofactors, yet metal utilization remains poorly mapped. Here, we present N-Zinclopedia, an atlas of predicted transition metal-binding sites and candidate metalloenzymes across protein fold space. N-Zinclopedia catalogs protein sites compatible with transition metal coordination, identified using ZincSight screening of protein structure model databases. We focused on previously uncharacterized domains and proteins, screening for transition metal-binding sites within over a million of these, spanning both poorly annotated and canonical folds. We also classified the predicted sites, using MAHOMES-II, as candidate catalytic or non-catalytic metal-binding sites. Experimental characterization of a previously unknown zinc binding site confirms that ZincSight can determine previously un-annotated zinc binding. N-Zinclopedia significantly expands the known landscape of metal utilization, providing numerous predictions that await experimental examination. N-Zinclopedia is available at: https://bentallab.github.io/nzinclopedia.

papers.title: PigGPA: A Domain-Constrained Agent for Porcine Genomic Breeding with Verifiable Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Large language model agents can plan and execute scientific analyses, but successful task completion does not establish whether analytical decisions remain consistent across independent sessions or whether computations follow the parameters specified beforehand. We investigated these limitations using four genomic analysis tasks. General-purpose agents showed limited consistency in analytical decisions across repeated sessions (57.5-58.8%). Incorporating domain knowledge improved analytical performance, with reusable skills increasing mean evaluation scores from 73.44 to 89.06/100 , but did not resolve decision variability or ensure agreement between specified and executed parameters. To address these limitations, we developed an approach combining domain-constrained analytical skills with call-level execution contracts. Each tool invocation is linked to a pre-execution parameter declaration through SHA-256 hashing, with actual command-line arguments and execution records subsequently checked against the declared parameters. We implemented this approach in PigGPA, an autonomous agent for porcine genomic breeding that integrates statistical genetics, sequence-based functional prediction and multi-omics annotation. PigGPA completed all benchmark tasks with full agreement between declared and executed parameters, while its core quantitative-genetic results closely matched established software (r = 0.999-1.000). An application to loin muscle depth further demonstrated an integrated workflow from genetic association analysis to functional interpretation. These findings show that domain knowledge improves analytical performance, while direct verification of tool execution provides an additional basis for reproducible scientific computation.

papers.title: U-Chrom: a unified framework for single-cell and spatial 3D genome data
papers.abstract: Single-cell Hi-C, spatial Hi-C and chromatin tracing measure the same genomes in incompatible formats. ChromData, one data model, indexes all three by cell and genomic bin; an open-source toolkit, linked browser and 22-dataset atlas build on it. Applied to ten mouse brain datasets of all three assays, the same calls rank cell types alike by short- over long-range proximity, and contact-based reconstructions largely place cell-type differences where imaging does.

papers.title: Enhancement of gut-microbiome-based classification of prodromal Parkinson's Disease cases by hyperparameter tuning, integration of multimodal data, and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is often preceded by a prodromal phase marked by non-motor symptoms such as REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder (RBD), gastrointestinal dysfunction, and olfactory impairment. Mounting evidence implicates gut microbiota in the early pathophysiology of PD. In this study, we aimed to enhance the classification of prodromal PD using gut microbiota profiles, with a focus on model performance and biomarker identification. Publicly available gut microbiome datasets of individuals with RBD and healthy controls were analyzed. Following batch correction and genus-level filtering, we identified six taxa significantly depleted in both RBD and PD groups, all belonging to short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera. Hyperparameter tuning on the testing set achieved an AUC of 0.889. When combining microbial and clinical features, the model achieved a peak mean AUC of 0.917. Feature selection identified 11 top-ranked features, yielding an AUC of 0.849. Using only the six differentially abundant SCFA-producing taxa, the model retained a strong predictive capacity with a mean AUC of 0.853. These results demonstrate the utility of gut microbiota, particularly SCFA-producing taxa, in the early identification of prodromal PD. Integration with select clinical features further improves model performance, supporting their potential role in early diagnostic frameworks.

papers.title: WispLab: open-source browser workbenches for laboratory image and qPCR analysis with reference-based verification
papers.abstract: Western blot densitometry, histological image quantification and relative qPCR analysis require choices about regions, backgrounds, thresholds, normalization and statistical comparisons. WispLab connects these operations in three open-source browser workbenches with Chinese and English interfaces, visible parameters and downloadable results. Routine quantitative processing runs locally; an optional external vision service in the Western blot tool is a separate data-transfer pathway. We assessed selected operations using separately implemented references and constructed inputs. For four public Western blot panels containing 21 measured lanes, local-background net signals and reference-lane ratios matched a Python reference at the recorded precision. A six-lane synthetic 16-bit design, duplicated in two files, yielded identical net signals in 12 measurements. Histology verification distinguished successful processing of 35 images from an H-DAB area comparison on eight images and ten regions. After correcting region matching and aligning preprocessing in the reference, positive-area fractions differed by at most 0.152 percentage points. qPCR verification used a public 60-well export and a constructed example; a fresh run of the fixed source version passed 422 specified checks after correction of a deep-tail defect in Dunnett-adjusted probabilities. These tests establish numerical agreement for specified inputs and methods, rather than biological accuracy, clinical validity or superiority over existing software. Source archives, comparison records and reproducible plotting scripts document the supported claims and the remaining validation gaps.

papers.title: Robust geometric drift correction and identity reconstruction for biological 3D time-lapse point clouds
papers.abstract: Structural time-lapse microscopy experiments aim to follow cells or subcellular structures over time, typically by detecting objects in each frame and linking them into trajectories. In practice, this process yields sequences of spatial coordinates derived from segmentation, while identity information across time is often absent or unreliable. In addition, the observed coordinates may be affected by systematic geometric drift. As a result, two coupled inference problems arise: geometric drift must be corrected, and object identities must be reconstructed from unlabeled point clouds. Here, we formulate both drift correction and identity reconstruction within a unified point-cloud framework and evaluate them jointly using controlled synthetic benchmarks and biological datasets. For drift correction, we compare rigid, local, and nonparametric models across spatially varying and non-rigid drift regimes. For identity reconstruction, we analyze a family of Hungarian assignment methods with constant-velocity refinement and different gating strategies, including innovation-based normalization. Across benchmarks, we find that increased model flexibility does not necessarily improve drift correction. A simple rigid stepwise model provides the most robust performance across a wide range of conditions, with a local community model as a competitive alternative under structured spatial heterogeneity. On the association side, innovation-based gating emerges as the key determinant of performance. Hungarian constant-velocity assignment with normalized innovation gating consistently outperforms coordinate-space variants, particularly under heterogeneous motion scales, birth and death processes, and density-induced ambiguity. Application to biological datasets confirms that the combined pipeline improves trajectory consistency and restores interpretable motion statistics, while highlighting the role of proxy references when ground truth is unavailable. Together, these results establish a practical and robust workflow for post hoc trajectory analysis in point-cloud-based time-lapse data, and clarify the methodological trade-offs between model expressivity and robustness in both drift correction and identity reconstruction.

papers.title: LineageFlow: Growth-Corrected State Dynamics for Probabilistic Cell-Fate Prediction
papers.abstract: Single-cell lineage tracing links early transcriptional states to the fates of their descendants, but forecasting clonal fate remains challenging because differentiation and unequal cell expansion jointly shape descendant populations. Here we introduce LineageFlow, a computational framework that combines continuous-time cell-state transitions, relative net growth and state-conditioned generative flows to predict future fate distributions and transcriptional profiles from early single-cell measurements. In clone-disjoint evaluations of lineage-traced hematopoiesis, LineageFlow improves fate prediction and expression-distribution accuracy over matched computational baselines. A separately retrained analysis of cord-blood lineage data shows a similar advantage at a longer prediction horizon. Controlled simulations show that accounting for differential growth improves fate prediction when descendant states expand at different rates, while offering little benefit under equal growth. These findings highlight the importance of modeling state transitions and relative expansion together when predicting the fate of unseen clones.

papers.title: Predicting Lifespan-Extending Compounds Using Supervised Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Identifying lifespan-extending compounds is an important objective in ageing research, but experimental screening remains costly and time consuming. This study evaluates supervised machine learning for predicting lifespan-extending compounds in Caenorhabditis elegans using compound-protein interaction features derived from the STITCH database. Three feature representations were compared: continuous interaction probabilities, binary features generated using a fixed threshold of 0.5, and binary features generated using an optimised threshold selected within cross-validation. Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with performance assessed by accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and area under the precision recall curve (AUPRC). Model interpretation was examined using Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI), SHAP, TreeSHAP, and LIME, with Jaccard similarity used to compare the top-ranked protein features. Random Forest achieved its highest accuracy (78.84%), AUROC (0.7391), and AUPRC (0.5202) using the fixed threshold binary representation. XGBoost achieved its highest accuracy (80.36%) using the optimised threshold representation, whereas continuous features yielded its highest AUROC (0.7605) and AUPRC (0.5332). SHAP and TreeSHAP showed the strongest agreement in protein rankings, producing identical top-10 feature sets across all three XGBoost representations. These findings demonstrate that feature representation influences both predictive performance and model interpretation, highlighting the importance of evaluating classification metrics alongside explainability when prioritising candidate compounds for further ageing research.

papers.title: Advances in 16S Taxonomic Classification: Impacts on Species-Level Resolution of Female Bladder Microbiota
papers.abstract: Bacteria are present in the human urinary bladder, even in the absence of infection. These bacteria comprise the urinary microbiome, or urobiome, and have the potential to promote bladder health or contribute to pathology. Despite its importance, studying the urobiome remains challenging given the high proportion of host to bacterial cells and low microbial biomass. The leading method for studying the urobiome has been 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. This culture-independent approach provides a cost-effective method for identifying bacteria, but taxonomic classification accuracy depends on three key factors: 1) the variable region targeted; 2) the reference database; and 3) the classification algorithm. In 2021, Hoffman et al. demonstrated that species-level classification of bladder microbiota was possible and that the database used was the most important factor, followed by the variable region. Here, we provide an updated analysis evaluating classification schemes using updated taxonomic databases, most notably GreenGenes2, and expand the analysis to full length 16S gene sequencing. We show that updated taxonomic reference databases improve the ability to identify bladder microbiota at the species level and that long-read sequencing of the full length 16S rRNA gene further improves species identification.

papers.title: HyARQ: a Snakemake workflow for allele-specific read counting and quality control in F1 hybrids
papers.abstract: Summary Allele-specific analysis in F1 hybrids allows direct assessment of how cis-regulatory variation contributes to differences in gene expression and other regulatory features. However, allele-specific analyses are sensitive to errors arising from multiple sources, including mapping bias and technical variation, requiring careful processing and quality control. These challenges are compounded by the fact that workflows for different molecular assays are often developed separately, making consistent analysis and quality control across assays difficult. Here, we introduce HyARQ, a Snakemake workflow for allele-specific read counting and quality control across RNA-seq, MOA-seq, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq data. HyARQ integrates assay-specific preprocessing, mapping to concatenated parental genomes, filtering, counting at paired parental genes or regulatory regions, and quality control within a common workflow. Using simulated datasets with known parental origin and allelic proportions, we show that HyARQ accurately recovers expected parental proportions with minimal cross-parent assignment across all four assay types. We further applied HyARQ to real RNA-seq, MOA-seq, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq datasets and generated paired parental counts and assay-specific quality control outputs for each assay. HyARQ provides a standardized and reproducible framework for allele-specific analysis across multiple molecular layers and facilitates downstream studies of cis-regulatory variation in F1 hybrids.

papers.title: TiSAM: fusing spatial and histopathology foundation models for whole-slide image segmentation
papers.abstract: Semantic segmentation of whole-slide images (WSIs) quantifies tissue composition and architecture, but existing models require extensive annotation and lose accuracy as the number of tissue classes increases or on heterogeneous, cross-scanner datasets. Here, we present the Tissue Segment Anything Model (TiSAM), which fuses SAM3 spatial features with UNI2-h pathology features within a multi-scale decoder. Because public benchmarks contain few tissue classes, we release MegaMouse, comprising 36,833 annotations of 52 tissue classes from 12 mouse organs, and an 11-class human pancreas dataset. TiSAM achieved the highest overall performance across four public datasets compared to existing convolutional neural network and vision transformer models, maintained high accuracy on MegaMouse, and maintained high accuracy in the human pancreas dataset when trained on as few as 5 annotated WSIs where previous integrations of SAM with pathology foundation models did not. TiSAM segmentations were also more consistent across eight slide scanners compared to other models. These results establish TiSAM as a general and highly adaptable framework for tissue segmentation, enabling studies containing many tissue classes, limited annotations, or images from multiple scanners.

papers.title: Spatial proteomic profiling of cardiac stromal populations and microenvironments in systemic sclerosis-associated primary myocardial involvement
papers.abstract: Objectives: To define cardiac stromal heterogeneity and spatial stromal-immune organization in systemic sclerosis-associated virus-negative myocarditis (SSc-VNM), a manifestation of primary SSc heart involvement. Methods: Imaging mass cytometry, a single-cell multiplexed spatial proteomic technology, was applied to endomyocardial biopsies from ten patients with SSc-VNM, seven with VNM associated with other systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (a-VNM) and nine with isolated VNM (i-VNM). Single-cell phenotyping, cellular-neighborhood and spatial-interaction analyses, and correlations with histological fibrosis were performed at patient level. Results: Among 82,673 segmented cells, we identified seven fibroblast phenotypes and one CD34+ stromal-cell population. The overall fibroblast/stromal compartment was expanded in SSc-VNM compared with i-VNM (adjusted p = 0.00973). The composition of fibroblasts/stromal cells differed profoundly in SSc-VNM compared with a-VNM and i-VNM, with numerical increases in CD34+ stromal cells and SOX9+ and PI16high/POSTNhigh fibroblasts and de-enrichment of FAPhigh/POSTNhigh fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. Spatial analysis identified ten cellular neighborhoods and revealed distinct SSc-VNM-associated patterns, including altered stromal-immune interaction networks. These included enriched interactions of CD34+ stromal cells and PI16high/POSTNhigh fibroblasts with CD163high/HLA-DR+ macrophages and CD68+ mast cells. PI16high/POSTNhigh and PI16-/POSTNhigh fibroblasts demonstrated the highest collagen type 1 expression among all stromal cell subsets across all VNM entities and PI16high/POSTNhigh fibroblasts were numerically increased in biopsies with [≥]10% fibrotic remodeling and were spatially associated with collagen-rich areas. Conclusions: Our findings refine current concepts of human fibrotic myocardial remodeling and support therapeutic targeting of specific stromal players such as POSTNhigh fibroblast subpopulations. Keywords: Systemic Sclerosis; Myocarditis; Myocardial Fibrosis; Fibroblasts; Imaging Mass Cytometry.

papers.title: A Sparse Modal Representation for Dolphin Echolocation Transients
papers.abstract: Characterising echolocation provides a non-invasive means of monitoring cetacean populations, health, and behaviour, offering critical data to inform conservation policy and mitigate the impacts of anthropogenic ocean noise. Echolocation clicks are short broadband transients whose internal oscillatory structure is difficult to compare in a sequence using conventional time- or frequency-domain representations. We introduce a Sparse Modal Representation (SMR) in which each click is described as a sparse superposition of delayed damped resonant modes. The representation separates resonant behaviour from temporal localisation, allowing both narrowband and broadband click components to emerge from the same set of resonant building blocks. The methodology combines Burg autoregressive pole estimation, sparse approximation in an over-complete dictionary, and nonlinear parameter refinement to obtain compact and interpretable modal descriptions of individual transients. The method is evaluated using recordings of free-ranging common dolphins (Delphinus delphis) from the DOLPHINFREE project in the Northern Bay of Biscay. The results demonstrate accurate reconstruction using a limited set of parameters that are repeatable across successive clicks and robust under realistic recording conditions. These conditions include wave, vessel, and sonar interference. Repeatability and robustness are essential for using this parameter set to detect changes in animal behaviour.

papers.title: Interactive Data Integrator for Uniform Data Processing in the MorPhiC Program
papers.abstract: We present an interactive Data Integrator to facilitate uniform data processing and integration with datasets generated by the NIH funded MorPhiC (Molecular Phenotypes of Null Alleles in Cells) program. In the dataset identification step, users can select published bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets generated by the MorPhiC program, specify external datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository, or upload raw RNA-seq data. Subsequently, users can select a subset of samples and indicate experimental design by assigning groups to samples. External data will then be processed using the MorPhiC approved bulk RNA-seq analytical pipeline, and differential expression will be inferred. Users also have the option to download the uniformly processed counts table.

papers.title: muDM: A Queryable Multi-Resolution Data Model for Vector Geometry in Spatial Bioimaging
papers.abstract: Spatial bioimaging combines raster imagery with vector geometries that encode molecular measurements, connectivity, and anatomical labels. A major challenge is to connect and jointly query these resources at scale, because the vector structures that locate them cannot be searched across resolutions. muDM is a spatial data model for associating vector geometry with its annotated records. Under a single schema, it arranges 2D and 3D geometries, together with their identities and measurements, as a precomputed multi-resolution pyramid, a columnar store that can be queried in place from object storage and equivalent render-ready tiles from the same index. Deployed in a public catalog containing more than 100 datasets, this single model supports connectome meshes, multiplexed tissue imaging, and spatial transcriptomics. For neuron meshes, classifiers which use geometry together with linked synapse counts exceed the performance of geometry-only models, while coarser levels preserved most balanced accuracy and using up to two orders of magnitude less stored geometry.

papers.title: Beyond Segmentation Accuracy: Evaluating Biological Fidelity in Spatial Pathology
papers.abstract: Multiplex immunofluorescence (MxIF) resolves cellular identity, state, and spatial organization within tumor tissue, enabling higher-order representations of cancer ecosystems including immune infiltration, multicellular neighborhoods, and tissue niches. Yet these analyses depend on a deceptively simple first step: accurately identifying individual cells. Segmentation errors can alter marker quantification, cellular phenotypes, cell-cell relationships, and ultimately the spatial organization inferred from an image. Consequently, improvements in conventional segmentation benchmarks matter biologically only if they propagate to more faithful representations of the tumor microenvironment. We test this relationship directly using an expert-curated benchmark of 31,924 expert-reviewed cells on three slides under a leave-slide-out protocol. We compare a domain-specific self-supervised encoder, adapted to multiplex tissue imaging, with supervised, microscopy-specific, prompted generalist, and general-purpose vision models, and pass every method's predicted cells through an identical downstream pipeline. We evaluate fidelity across four levels: cell segmentation, phenotype assignment, spatial neighborhood structure, and tissue organization, comprising niches and tumor-immune interactions. The resulting hierarchy reveals that these levels do not improve in lockstep. Cellular phenotype assignment is comparatively robust to segmentation differences, whereas missed cells increasingly disrupt neighborhood structure and tumor-immune interactions. As a stringent spatial-interaction test, tumor-CD8+ contact recovery is poorly predicted by conventional segmentation quality (Panoptic Quality: {rho} = 0.18), while errors specifically at tumor-immune interfaces are strongly associated with contact fidelity ({rho} = -0.80). Methods with nearly identical segmentation accuracy can therefore produce substantially different biological representations. These results argue that cell segmentation for spatial pathology should be evaluated not only by boundary and instance accuracy, but also by preservation of the biological relationships that downstream analyses are intended to measure.

papers.title: Network organization of protein binding-site landscapes across scales
papers.abstract: Studying protein binding sites helps explain ligand recognition and selectivity, informing drug development and repurposing. Here, we combine protein language model embeddings with network analysis to investigate how local recognition environments organize across scales. We represented 121,673 non-redundant, experimentally identified binding sites using ProtT5 embeddings of ligand-contacting residues and constructed a mutual nearest-neighbor network. Embedding proximity was associated with local structural similarity, supporting the structural relevance of network relationships. Globally, the network exhibited ligand-related organization. At the mesoscopic scale, communities revealed heterogeneous landscapes within established protein classifications, with InterPro categories ranging from compact neighborhoods to dispersed recognition environments. Focusing on kinases, a major class of drug targets, we found that communities within individual proteins distinguished separate binding regions and resolved recurrent residue-defined microenvironments within broad structural classes. Local similarities also connected sites in proteins with low sequence identity and non-overlapping InterPro annotations, suggesting shared recognition features across distant proteins. Together, these results show how network organization captures both diversification within protein categories and local similarities across their boundaries. This multiscale framework complements conventional protein classifications and provides a basis for prioritizing structural and biochemical investigations of ligand cross-reactivity, selectivity, and repurposing opportunities.

papers.title: StainAI-Web: An Interactive Platform for Whole-Slide Microglial Morphology Analysis
papers.abstract: Microglial morphology analysis has emerged as a critical approach in neuroinflammation research. The increasing availability of high-resolution and whole-slide histology images has created strong demand for robust, scalable analytical methods capable of efficiently processing these datasets. Existing approaches may require code-based local computation or prolonged processing times for whole-slide images, while manual morphology quantification remains labor-intensive. To address these limitations, we introduce StainAI-Web, a server that performs rapid, automated microglial morphology detection across whole-slide immunohistochemistry images in the cloud. The system provides interactive grayscale preprocessing and supports ROI-based regional quantification, allowing users to define specific tissue regions and systematically compare microglial populations across regions. An interactive visualization module dynamically updates quantitative summaries of morphological distributions as ROIs are selected or modified. Analysis results, including structured JSON files and morphology-annotated overlays, are downloadable for downstream analysis or integration into external computational pipelines. These integrated features provide an accessible framework for efficient and reproducible whole-slide microglial morphology analysis. The StainAI-Web is available at https://stainaiviewer.azurewebsites.net/.

papers.title: Phase-Based Frequency Tracking and Analysis of Vocalisations in the Genus Saxicola
papers.abstract: Acoustic analysis provides valuable tools for studying bird vocalisations, but quantitative characterisation of call structure remains challenging when frequency and amplitude vary jointly over time. We present a phase-based frequency tracking method that represents amplitude as a function of instantaneous frequency and use it to characterise alarm calls in the genus Saxicola. The method enables the extraction of acoustic features describing the frequency trajectory and temporal structure of individual calls. We apply the method to a dataset of 801 calls from 49 recordings representing 15 species, and use principal component analysis (PCA) and robust PCA to investigate patterns of acoustic variation across species, recordings and geographic regions. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the approach and reveal structured patterns of acoustic similarity and variation among the calls analysed. Robust PCA concentrates the variance of the low-rank representation into fewer principal components than conventional PCA applied to the original feature matrix, providing a complementary representation of the dominant acoustic structure. The observed patterns illustrate the potential of quantitative acoustic characterisation for comparative studies of vocal variation. However, uneven species representation and uncertainty in individual identity and taxonomic labels limit the biological conclusions that can be drawn from the present dataset. The method provides a foundation for further acoustic research, in which broader sampling and integration with independent genetic and morphological evidence could help investigate variation within and among species.

papers.title: Latent-Factor Stability Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating SABLE-MO in Simulated and Cancer Multi-Omics Data
papers.abstract: Reproducibility is often used to assess latent factors learned from multi-omics data. Yet factors that recur across model refits may not reflect the shared biological structure of interest. We investigated this issue using SABLE-MO, a shared/private representation-learning framework with a sep-arate factor-retention procedure. We evaluated the method in simulations with known latent structure. The original retention rule produced no false biological shared-factor acceptance across 800 independent-null datasets, but accepted at least one false factor in 70 of 200 correlated-private datasets (35%). Following an exploratory analysis of this failure, we increased the lower-decile aligned-correlation threshold from 0.40 to 0.60 and tested it on a new, independently seeded simulation bank. False acceptance decreased from 33% to 19%, while recovery of true shared factors changed only slightly (94.375% to 94.0%). Exact modality-support attribution reached 67.5%, below its prespecified criterion. We also analyzed matched RNA expression, DNA methylation, and copy- number data from TARGET osteosarcoma (78 patients), TCGA-SARC (250), and TCGA-KIRC (304). Outcome-blind model selec- tion favored a simpler shared/private representation in TARGET.In both TCGA cohorts, the more complex representation improved cross-view retrieval and missing-view reconstruction relative to the simpler model, but worsened ordinary reconstruction. These external comparisons were performed before factor retention. Our results show that factor reproducibility, representation quality,and biological interpretation require separate assessment. Stricter retention reduced errors in a specific simulated setting but did not eliminate them

papers.title: Hierarchical distribution matching enables comprehensive characterization of common and condition-specific cell niches in spatial omics data
papers.abstract: Deciphering cell niches in complex tissues is essential for understanding tissue structure and disease. Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled subcellular resolution and accurate cell identity mapping. However, robust delineation of cell niches and disease-associated spatial patterns remains difficult. We introduce Harmonics, a novel computational framework that systematically identifies both common and condition-specific cell niches from spatial omics data through hierarchical distribution matching. Harmonics also includes a suite of downstream modules that facilitate comprehensive niche characterization. We demonstrate its scalability, accuracy and generalizability across datasets spanning diverse species, tissues, diseases, spatial modalities, and technological platforms. For condition-agnostic datasets, Harmonics outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and robustness, and further demonstrates the capability to resolve niche structures at finer granularity. Across diverse diseases including pulmonary fibrosis, triple-negative breast cancer, and colorectal cancer, Harmonics enables precise identification of condition-specific niches and reveals disease-associated dynamics, subtype-specific spatial patterns, and structured immune architectures. We envision Harmonics as a practical and versatile tool for spatial niche analysis that can be applied across a wide range of biological contexts and seamlessly integrated with existing spatial omics workflows.

papers.title: An integrated database of ion channels
papers.abstract: Ion channels play critical roles in a wide range of physiological processes, including the propagation of nerve impulses, insulin secretion and regulation of heart rate. Alterations in ion-channels function or expression can contribute to the development of various diseases, including cancers, genetic disorders, and infectious diseases. Ion channels represent the second-largest class of membrane proteins considered potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, a comprehensive data resource integrating information on human ion channels and their associations with diseases has been limited. Therefore, the Integrated Database of Ion Channels (IDIC) was developed, comprising information on 493 human ion channels. The database contains a broad range of ion-channel annotations, including gene and protein information, structural details, protein signature sequences, protein domains, nuclear localization signals, and signal peptides. It also provides cross-references to several established biological resources, including the Human Genome Organization Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC), National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene, Vertebrate Genome Annotation (VEGA), Ensembl, and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Furthermore, IDIC incorporates genomic variations identified in various tumors and disease associations involving ion channels, which have been systematically curated from published literature. Through concise search methods and user-friendly browsing functionalities, IDIC serves as an integrated resource for exploring human ion channels and investigating their structural, functional, genetic, and disease-related characteristics. Thus, the database can facilitate a better understanding of ion channels and their potential involvement in diverse human diseases.

papers.title: Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.

papers.title: Metalink: Joint taxonomic and functional profiling of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes across resolution scales
papers.abstract: Metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses remain largely fragmented: taxonomic and functional profiling are performed separately, often at a single resolution (reads, contigs, or MAGs) yielding separate species or function lists rather than mechanistic insights. Here, we developed Metalink, a tool that unifies taxonomic and functional profiling into coupled outputs across all three resolution levels. Metalink is built on three innovations. First, we constructed a Last Common Function-based functional Hierarchy (LCFH) from ~424 million proteins, organizing KEGG Orthologs into a tree structure that enables LCA-like functional assignment. Second, a unified framework integrates the taxonomy of Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB), the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), and NCBI for consistent classification across reads, contigs, and MAGs. Third, a multi-level integration strategy with overlap-based deduplication balances accuracy and completeness. At the read level, Metalink exceeds both HUMAnN3 and eggNOG-Mapper in functional assignment accuracy while running ~30-fold faster and 1,000-fold faster, respectively; at the contig level, its functional profiles remain highly consistent with eggNOG-Mapper. Multi-level integration further improves taxonomic resolution over single-level analyses and outperforms leading taxonomic profilers on the CAMI II benchmarks. Metalink's joint outputs move the analysis of metagenomes and metatranscriptomes from cataloging species and functions toward mechanistic inference of species-function-environment triadic associations. By enabling these integrated analyses across resolution scales, Metalink provides a general framework for linking community composition to its functional potential across diverse ecosystems.

papers.title: RiboBridge couples RNA backbone generation to sequence design through a learned interaction topology
papers.abstract: Designing ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules with prescribed structures and functions is central to RNA engineering. Backbone-first approaches generate three-dimensional geometry before assigning a nucleotide sequence, yet leave open how that geometry should be represented for downstream sequence design. Here we introduce RiboBridge, which infers a probabilistic residue-pair state from backbone geometry, recycles binary pair probabilities through a second pass and transfers binary and typed signals as soft attention biases for sequence decoding. On 550 generated backbones, pair-type decoding achieved joint refolding validity of 0.451 versus 0.335 for an architecture-matched topology-free decoder. On a matched 110-backbone intervention cohort, replacing aligned pair states with exact-length donors matched on pair-state statistics reduced joint validity from 0.464 to 0.214, showing backbone alignment matters. Pair-confidence ranking enriched the joint-validity rate from 0.451 overall to 0.596 among the top 248 before external refolding, with the same ranking signal transferring to independently generated RFDpoly and RNA-FrameFlow backbones. On 53 experimentally determined backbones, pair-coupled decoding improved secondary-structure agreement relative to residue-wise argmax. These results support a learned relational interface between sequence-free backbone generation and sequence design.

papers.title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
papers.abstract: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.

papers.title: DIMPLE: A Tree-Guided Divide-and-Conquer Framework for ILS-Aware Phylogenetic Network Inference on Large-Scale Data
papers.abstract: Inferring evolutionary histories of species provides a foundation for comparative genomics and evolutionary analyses. Extensive evidence of reticulate evolution motivates the inference of phylogenetic networks, which represent relationships that species trees cannot capture. However, accurate reconstruction of large phylogenetic networks remains a major challenge because of the vast space of possible network topologies. Here, we propose DIMPLE, a divide-and-conquer framework for phylogenetic network inference without an explicit restriction on network level. DIMPLE uses a tree-of-blobs (TOB), which represents the tree-like relationships between regions of potential reticulation while leaving relationships within those regions unresolved. Within each unresolved region, DIMPLE partitions the set of taxa into pairwise-disjoint subsets, each containing at most a user-specified number of taxa. Multiple division runs are allowed, and subsets from different runs may overlap. DIMPLE infers a subnetwork on each subset, merges the subnetworks within each region, and uses the TOB to assemble the resulting networks into a network on the full taxon set. Experiments with true inputs demonstrate accurate merging, with improved reticulation recovery over existing methods on higher-level networks. With estimated inputs, DIMPLE achieves competitive topological accuracy and more consistently recovers hybrid ancestry than competing methods across varying levels of network complexity. Its computational requirements support analyses of hundreds of taxa. Applications to fern and gymnosperm datasets recover documented hybridization and previously reported phylogenetic conflict.

papers.title: Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Networks for Antibody Sequence-Structure Co-Design
papers.abstract: Motivation: The design of antibody complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) is pivotal for therapeutic development, yet remains challenged by the complexity of the antibody-antigen interface. Existing methods, which largely rely on pairwise relationships, struggle to capture intrinsic multi-body interactions and global structural constraints. Results: We propose the Relation-Aware Graph-Hypergraph Network (RA-GHN), a framework that unifies graph-based pairwise modeling with biophysical hypergraphs to capture high-order cooperative effects. Its heterogeneous hypergraph uses epitope-paratope interaction patches, spatial structural clusters, and high-degree hub structures. A dual-pathway architecture integrates a Relation-Aware Equivariant Graph Network with an Equivariant Hypergraph Encoder while preserving SE(3)-equivariance. We also introduce the Structure-Sequence Decoupling Index, which balances structural reliability with sequence novelty. Experiments show that RA-GHN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across standard benchmarks and affinity optimization tasks.
